The sum is the hyper-Wiener index 46.0, against a Wiener index of 28." width="100%"} The hyper-Wiener index (Randić, 1993) refines the Wiener index by also summing squared distances, so far-apart pairs weigh more heavily: `WW(G) = ½ Σ_{u < v} (d(u, v) + d(u, v)²)` Equivalently, `½ d (d + 1)` is the number of sub-paths of a shortest path of length `d`, so the index counts, over all pairs, the paths contained in their shortest paths (Klein, Lukovits and Gutman, 1995). Like `wiener_index()`, it is a topological descriptor in chemistry, where it correlates with boiling points and other properties of molecules; the square term makes it more sensitive to a molecule's elongation. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weighted]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True`, edge weights (`1` where missing) are the distances. If `False`, every edge has distance `1`. If `None` (default), follows whether the graph was created as weighted. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The hyper-Wiener index. Returns `0.0` for graphs with fewer than two nodes and infinity (`float('inf')`) for disconnected graphs. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is directed. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} The sum runs over unordered pairs, as in Randić's and Klein et al.'s definition and in `wiener_index()`, which gives the values tabulated in the chemistry literature (15 for the 4-node path, butane's carbon skeleton). NetworkX's `hyper_wiener_index()` sums over ordered pairs while keeping the factor of one half, so its values are exactly twice these (30 for the 4-node path). Distances come from a breadth-first search from every node, or Dijkstra's algorithm with `weighted=True`, in $O(V(V + E))$ or $O(V(V + E) \log V)$ time. ## Examples {.doc-examples} On a 4-node path the distances are 1 (three pairs), 2 (two pairs) and 3 (one pair), so `WW = ½ (3 · 2 + 2 · 6 + 1 · 12) = 15`; the Wiener index is 10: ::: {#5b0368c5 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec path = ec.Graph().add_path_graph(4) path.wiener_index(), path.hyper_wiener_index() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` (10.0, 15.0) ``` ::: ::: Among trees on the same number of nodes, the star is the most compact and the path the least: ::: {#9914655e .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} star = ec.Graph().add_star_graph(6) line = ec.Graph().add_path_graph(6) star.hyper_wiener_index(), line.hyper_wiener_index() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (35.0, 70.0) ``` ::: :::
